name: Hierarchical Clustering
when_to_use: Metric variables, no dependent variable (unsupervised); groups by distance matrix (Euclidean) and linkage method (single/complete/average/ward.D); number of groups decided from the dendrogram.

expected_input.question: How to group observations by similarity?

plain_explanation.purpose: Joins similar items into groups, from most to least similar, forming a tree of groupings.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When you want to discover natural groups but do not know how many exist, and the dataset is small or medium.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A table with one item per row and several numeric measures per column (e.g., spending, age, frequency).
plain_explanation.example: Group similar municipalities on education indicators to compare each only with its peers.
plain_explanation.diagram: A B C D E  ->  (A B) (D E) C  ->  ((A B) C) (D E)  ->  all together

name: Non-hierarchical Clustering (k-means / DBSCAN)
when_to_use: Standardized metric variables; k-means requires the number of clusters defined a priori, DBSCAN groups by density without defining k; preferable to hierarchical on larger datasets.

expected_input.question: How to group observations by similarity?

plain_explanation.purpose: Splits items into a number of groups you choose (k-means) or into regions of high concentration (DBSCAN).
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When the dataset is large and you already have an idea of how many groups you want, or want to isolate cases that belong to no group.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A table with one item per row and numeric columns, preferably on the same scale.
plain_explanation.example: Split customers into 4 purchase profiles; or find suppliers with out-of-pattern behavior.
plain_explanation.diagram: loose points -> random centers -> each point goes to the nearest center -> centers adjust -> repeat

name: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
when_to_use: Metric variables correlated with one another; reduces dimensionality without assuming a theoretical latent structure; adequacy checked by KMO and Bartlett's test of sphericity before extracting components.

expected_input.question: What is the dimensionality reduction that preserves variance?

plain_explanation.purpose: Summarizes many correlated columns into a few 'overall scores', losing as little information as possible.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When there are many measures that say almost the same thing and you want to trim down or draw everything on a 2D chart.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A table with several numeric columns correlated with each other; at least a few dozen rows.
plain_explanation.example: Reduce 20 social indicators of each city to 2 axes to plot on a position map.
plain_explanation.diagram: 20 columns  ->  [PCA]  ->  2 axes (score 1, score 2) + how much each axis explains

name: Simple Correspondence Analysis (CA)
when_to_use: Two categorical variables (two-way contingency table); association tested by chi-square before generating the perceptual map.

expected_input.question: What is the association between two categorical variables?

plain_explanation.purpose: Shows on a map the relationship between two categories of a count table (who 'goes with' whom).
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When you have two categorical variables (e.g., region x product) and want to see associations visually.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A table of counts crossing two categorical variables.
plain_explanation.example: See which regions buy more of which product types, on a single map.
plain_explanation.diagram: Rows and columns become points on the same plane; close points = strong association

name: Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA)
when_to_use: Three or more categorical variables simultaneously, when a single contingency table is not possible.

expected_input.question: What is the association structure among categorical variables?

plain_explanation.purpose: Makes the same map as correspondence analysis, but for several categorical variables at once.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When there are several multiple-choice questionnaires and you want to see which answers appear together.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A table with one respondent per row and several categorical columns (text or codes).
plain_explanation.example: See the answer profile of a satisfaction survey: whoever chooses 'excellent' also chooses what?
plain_explanation.diagram: answers to several questions -> single map: close answers appear together

name: Simple Linear Regression
when_to_use: Continuous metric dependent variable, one metric predictor, linear relationship, normal and homoscedastic residuals.

expected_input.question: What is the linear relationship between the dependent variable and the predictors?

plain_explanation.purpose: Measures how much one thing changes when another changes, and draws the best line linking the two.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When you want to predict a number from a single factor.
plain_explanation.data_needed: Two numeric columns: what you want to predict and the factor that explains it.
plain_explanation.example: Estimate monthly sales from ad investment.
plain_explanation.diagram:
sales ^   . .  /
      |  . /.
      +------> ads  (line that best fits the points)

name: Multiple Linear Regression
when_to_use: Continuous metric dependent variable, two or more predictors (metric and/or dummies); check multicollinearity (VIF/tolerance), stepwise selection, Box-Cox when residuals are not normal.

expected_input.question: What is the linear relationship between the dependent variable and the predictors?

plain_explanation.purpose: Predicts a number using several factors at once and shows the weight of each.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When more than one factor influences the result and you want to separate the effect of each.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A numeric column to predict and two or more factor columns; a few dozen rows at minimum.
plain_explanation.example: Estimate a company's revenue by size, sector and region, seeing how much each one weighs.
plain_explanation.diagram: price = base + a*size + b*age + c*neighborhood

name: Binary Logistic Regression
when_to_use: Binary dependent variable (0/1); evaluation by log-likelihood, AIC/BIC, pseudo-R² and ROC curve.

expected_input.question: How to predict the probability of a category?

plain_explanation.purpose: Calculates the chance of something happening or not (yes/no) from factors.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When the outcome is of two types: bought/did not buy, paid/did not pay.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A response column with two values (0/1) and factor columns.
plain_explanation.example: Estimate the chance of a quote becoming a sale based on value and channel.
plain_explanation.diagram: factors -> [model] -> chance from 0% to 100% -> cutoff (e.g., above 50% = yes)

name: Multinomial Logistic Regression
when_to_use: Nominal categorical dependent variable with three or more unordered categories.

expected_input.question: How to predict the probability of a category?

plain_explanation.purpose: Calculates the chance of each of several possible categories (more than two) from factors.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When the outcome is a choice among three or more options with no natural order.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A categorical response column with 3+ values and factor columns.
plain_explanation.example: Predict which of 3 plans a customer will choose, based on their profile.
plain_explanation.diagram: factors -> [model] -> chance of plan A, B and C (sum to 100%)

name: Poisson Regression
when_to_use: Count dependent variable (integer, non-negative), assuming equidispersion (mean approximately equal to variance).

expected_input.question: How to model a count dependent variable with equidispersion?

plain_explanation.purpose: Predicts counts (how many times something happens) from factors.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When the outcome is a small integer: occurrences, calls, defects per period.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A column with counts (0, 1, 2...) and factor columns.
plain_explanation.example: Estimate the number of support tickets per week according to customer size.
plain_explanation.diagram: factors -> [model] -> expected count (e.g., 3.2 per week)

name: Negative Binomial Regression
when_to_use: Count dependent variable with overdispersion (variance greater than the mean), when Poisson does not fit.

expected_input.question: How to model counts with overdispersion?

plain_explanation.purpose: Predicts counts like Poisson, but tolerates very 'spread out' data (many zeros and a few huge values).
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When counts vary far more than normal, and Poisson becomes too optimistic.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A column of integer counts and factor columns.
plain_explanation.example: Predict how many documents each legislator issues per month, when a few issue almost everything.
plain_explanation.diagram: Poisson: narrow bars | Negative binomial: bars with a long right tail

name: Zero-inflated models (ZIP / ZINB)
when_to_use: Count dependent variable with excess zeros beyond what Poisson or Negative Binomial predicts.

expected_input.question: How to model counts with excess zeros?

plain_explanation.purpose: Predicts counts when there are excess zeros, treating 'never happens' separately from 'sometimes happens'.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When most items have zero and you need to understand why there are so many zeros.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A column of counts with many zeros and factor columns.
plain_explanation.example: Count accidents per company, where many companies never have any because of safety policy.
plain_explanation.diagram: item -> is it in the 'always zero' group? yes: 0 | no: normal count (0, 1, 2...)

name: Multilevel Model HLM2 (2 levels)
when_to_use: Hierarchical data on 2 levels (e.g., students within schools), metric dependent variable; decomposes within- and between-group variance (ICC).

expected_input.question: How to decompose variance between and within hierarchical levels?

plain_explanation.purpose: Does regression while respecting that items live in groups (group effect + individual effect).
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When the data are nested on two levels and items in the same group resemble each other.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A table with one item per row, a column telling the group and factor columns for both levels.
plain_explanation.example: Explain student scores taking each student's school into account.
plain_explanation.diagram: Level 2: school -> Level 1: students within the school

name: Multilevel Model HLM3 (3 levels)
when_to_use: Hierarchical data on 3 levels (e.g., repeated measures within students within schools).
r_functions: manual computation of ICC and predictions from a pre-fitted lme() object

expected_input.question: How to decompose variance between and within hierarchical levels?
expected_input.note: Needs adaptation before running (see the notes field).

plain_explanation.purpose: Same as the two-level one, but with three layers of groups nested within each other.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When there are three levels: for example student, school and municipality.
plain_explanation.data_needed: One row per item, columns identifying the two groups above and factors for the three levels.
plain_explanation.example: Explain student scores considering school and municipality at the same time.
plain_explanation.diagram: municipality -> schools -> students

name: Exponential Smoothing (SES / Holt / Holt-Winters / ETS)
when_to_use: Univariate time series; SES for constant level without trend/seasonality, Holt for trend, Holt-Winters/ETS for trend + seasonality.

expected_input.question: How to smooth and extrapolate a time series?

plain_explanation.purpose: Forecasts the future of a series over time, giving more weight to recent data.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When there is a monthly or weekly series with trend and/or seasonality and you want a quick, simple forecast.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A column of values in time sequence, with regular dates; at least 2 complete cycles.
plain_explanation.example: Forecast sales for the next 6 months.
plain_explanation.diagram: past ------[more weight on recent]------> forecast

name: ARIMA
when_to_use: Stationary time series (or made stationary via differencing/Box-Cox), with relevant autocorrelation in the residuals.

expected_input.question: How to model a time series with autocorrelation?

plain_explanation.purpose: Forecasts a series using its own past behavior (inertia, corrections, shocks).
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When the series depends on its past and you want a model more flexible than smoothing.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A column of values over time, at regular intervals, preferably 30+ points.
plain_explanation.example: Forecast next month's ticket volume.
plain_explanation.diagram: past values + past errors -> next value

name: Prophet
when_to_use: Time series with multiple seasonality/holidays and nonlinear trend; robust to outliers and missing data.

expected_input.question: How to forecast a time series with multiple seasonality?
expected_input.note: Needs adaptation before running (see the notes field).

plain_explanation.purpose: Forecasts series with strong seasonality and holidays, automatically and with little configuration.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When the series has a weekly/yearly pattern, gaps in the data or special dates.
plain_explanation.data_needed: Two columns: date and value; ideally months or years of history.
plain_explanation.example: Forecast daily visits to a website, with peaks on commemorative dates.
plain_explanation.diagram: series = trend + seasonality + holidays

name: Decision Tree / Regression Tree (CART)
when_to_use: Categorical (classification) or continuous (regression) dependent variable; tabular data, no normality/linearity requirement; overfitting controlled via pruning (cp) and train-test validation.

expected_input.question: How to predict with a decision-tree-based model?

plain_explanation.purpose: Generates a sequence of yes/no questions leading to a decision or prediction.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When you need a rule that is easy to explain and draw.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A table with the response (category or number) and factor columns.
plain_explanation.example: Decide whether a customer is at high risk of canceling, through simple questions about usage and tenure.
plain_explanation.diagram:
age > 30?
 yes -> income > 5k? ... | no -> ...

name: Bootstrapping (confidence interval by resampling)
when_to_use: Estimate the sampling distribution/confidence interval of a statistic (e.g., quantile, mean) without assuming normality; any numeric variable.

expected_input.question: What is the confidence interval of a statistic without assuming normality?

plain_explanation.purpose: Estimates the uncertainty of a result by drawing data from the dataset itself many times.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When you want a confidence interval without relying on formulas that assume the shape of the data.
plain_explanation.data_needed: Any table; works even with few rows.
plain_explanation.example: Give an interval for the conversion rate of a small sample of opportunities.
plain_explanation.diagram: dataset -> resample with replacement 1000x -> compute 1000x -> range holding 95%

name: Bagging / Random Forest
when_to_use: Categorical or continuous dependent variable; reduces the variance of unstable trees; robust to outliers and nonlinearity; needs a medium/large dataset.

expected_input.question: How to reduce the variance of unstable models with multiple trees?

plain_explanation.purpose: Trains many different trees and uses their vote, giving more stable predictions.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When you want good accuracy without much tuning and with varied data.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A table with the response and several factor columns; hundreds of rows or more.
plain_explanation.example: Score the prospecting potential of each company.
plain_explanation.diagram: tree 1, tree 2, ... tree 500 -> vote -> final answer

name: Manual Boosting (gradient on residuals)
when_to_use: Continuous dependent variable; illustrates the boosting principle (sequential fitting of residuals) before using ready-made gbm/xgboost.

expected_input.question: How to improve prediction by sequentially fitting residuals?

plain_explanation.purpose: Builds a model in stages, each one correcting the errors of the previous.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When you want to understand in practice how boosting works, before using a library.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A table with the response and factor columns.
plain_explanation.example: Improve step by step the default forecast, correcting the badly predicted cases.
plain_explanation.diagram: model 1 -> errors -> model 2 focuses on the errors -> model 3 ...

name: XGBoost
when_to_use: Categorical or continuous dependent variable; large data volumes, tolerates nonlinearity and interaction between variables; requires tuning (grid/cv).

expected_input.question: How to improve prediction by sequentially fitting residuals?

plain_explanation.purpose: Makes very accurate predictions by combining small trees that correct each other in sequence.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When accuracy matters more than explanation and there is plenty of tabular data.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A table with response and factors, hundreds of rows or more.
plain_explanation.example: Predict the sale probability of each opportunity to order the contact queue.
plain_explanation.diagram: tree 1 + tree 2 + ... + tree N = final prediction

name: Artificial Neural Network / Perceptron (neuralnet)
when_to_use: Continuous (regression) or categorical (classification) dependent variable; standardized numeric predictors (0-1); compared in the material against Random Forest.

expected_input.question: How to model nonlinear relationships with a simple neural network?

plain_explanation.purpose: Minimal neural network, a single neuron, that learns to separate two classes with a line.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: To learn the basic concept of a neural network or separate simple cases.
plain_explanation.data_needed: Numeric factor columns and a response with two classes.
plain_explanation.example: Classify messages as urgent or not, from two measures.
plain_explanation.diagram: inputs x weights -> sum -> exceeds threshold? -> yes/no

name: Neural Network implemented from scratch (no framework)
when_to_use: Teaching purposes; continuous dependent variable (e.g., wine quality); illustrates forward/backward propagation and gradient manually, without keras/tensorflow.
r_functions: custom functions (getLayerSize, initializeParameters, sigmoid, forwardPropagation, backwardPropagation, updateParameters, trainModel) — base R only

expected_input.question: How to understand forward/backward propagation manually?
expected_input.note: Needs adaptation before running (see the notes field).

plain_explanation.purpose: Neural network built by hand, to understand how it learns by adjusting weights.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: To study the inner workings, not for production.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A numeric table of factors and a response.
plain_explanation.example: Watch, step by step, a network learn to predict a score.
plain_explanation.diagram: input -> hidden layer -> output -> error -> correct the weights -> repeat

name: Multilayer Neural Network (neuralnet) — regression and classification
when_to_use: Continuous (e.g., property value) or binary (e.g., admission) dependent variable; comparison with CART tree; architecture with multiple hidden layers.

expected_input.question: How to model complex relationships with a multilayer neural network?

plain_explanation.purpose: Neural network with intermediate layers, which learns complex relationships among the factors.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When the relationship between factors and response is complicated and there is plenty of data.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A numeric table with a response; thousands of rows help.
plain_explanation.example: Predict a building's energy consumption from weather and occupancy.
plain_explanation.diagram: inputs -> layer 1 -> layer 2 -> output

name: Recurrent Neural Network (RNN)
when_to_use: Sequential/time-series data (e.g., climate humidity, stock price); continuous dependent variable; requires normalization (0-1) and formatting into a matrix by time steps.

expected_input.question: How to model nonlinear relationships with a simple neural network?

plain_explanation.purpose: Neural network that reads sequences keeping a memory of what it saw before.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When order matters: series over time or text.
plain_explanation.data_needed: Ordered sequences, such as values over time or words in a sentence.
plain_explanation.example: Predict the next value of a series from the last 30 days.
plain_explanation.diagram: step 1 -> step 2 -> step 3 (each passes memory to the next)

name: Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) / Deep Belief Network (DBN)
when_to_use: Unsupervised/generative learning for images (reconstruction) and multiclass classification (e.g., MNIST/Fashion-MNIST digits); multilevel categorical dependent variable.

expected_input.question: How to learn unsupervised representations of images?
expected_input.note: Needs adaptation before running (see the notes field).

plain_explanation.purpose: Network that learns hidden patterns in the data on its own, with no labeled response needed.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: To extract features automatically before classifying, or to study the subject.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A numeric table of factors, with no response column required.
plain_explanation.example: Discover recurring purchase patterns before building a model.

name: Web Scraping
when_to_use: Extraction of unstructured data from HTML pages (text, tables); not a statistical technique in itself, but a collection step before any analysis.
notes: Depends on internet access at run time — not a code failure.

expected_input.question: How to extract structured data from HTML pages?

plain_explanation.data_needed: Addresses (URLs) of the pages and the description of the section to collect.

name: Basic Text Mining (tokenization, stopwords, wordcloud, n-grams, word correlation)
when_to_use: Text corpus (e.g., Project Gutenberg books); preliminary steps before any text modeling — tokenization, removal of stopwords/accents, stemming, bigrams, correlation between words.
notes: Depends on internet access for gutenberg_download().

expected_input.question: What are the preliminary steps for analyzing a text corpus?

plain_explanation.purpose: Prepares and counts words in texts to discover what is being talked about.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: As the first step of any text analysis.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A column with free text, one document per row.
plain_explanation.example: Discover the most cited terms in expense descriptions.
plain_explanation.diagram: text -> split words -> remove empty words -> count

name: TF-IDF (Term Frequency - Inverse Document Frequency)
when_to_use: Identify the most important/distinctive words per document within a corpus (comparing two or more documents); the variable is term frequency per document.
notes: Depends on internet access for gutenberg_download().

expected_input.question: Which words most distinguish documents in a corpus?

plain_explanation.purpose: Gives each word an importance score: high if frequent in one text and rare in the others.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When you want to find the words that truly characterize each document.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A text column, one document per row.
plain_explanation.example: Find the terms that distinguish each group of complaints.
plain_explanation.diagram: word common to all -> low score | word only in this text -> high score

name: Lexicon-based Sentiment Analysis (AFINN/Bing/NRC dictionaries)
when_to_use: Polarity/emotion of text via a join with a ready-made lexicon, with no labeled/training data needed; English corpus in the material (e.g., Jane Austen novels).

expected_input.question: What is the polarity/emotion of a text?

plain_explanation.purpose: Measures whether a text is positive or negative by summing scores of words from a dictionary.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When you want an opinion thermometer without labeling anything.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A text column and a dictionary of words with scores.
plain_explanation.example: Measure the tone of customer reviews.
plain_explanation.diagram: 'great' +2, 'delay' -1  ->  sum = +1  ->  positive

name: Text Classification (Naive Bayes on a document-term matrix)
when_to_use: Supervised classification of sentiment/category (e.g., positive/negative) with labeled data; binary categorical dependent variable; requires a clean corpus (stopwords, stemming) and a sparse document-term matrix.

expected_input.question: How to classify documents with a probabilistic model?

plain_explanation.purpose: Classifies texts into categories by learning from already labeled examples.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When there are texts with a known category and you want to classify the new ones.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A text column and a column with the correct category, with a reasonable volume of examples.
plain_explanation.example: Classify an expense description by type.
plain_explanation.diagram: words of the text -> chance of each category -> the highest wins

name: Linear Programming (objective function and constraints formulation)
when_to_use: Optimization problem with a linear objective function and linear constraints (e.g., maximize revenue subject to limited resources); conceptual material, no solver implementation in R.

expected_input.question: How to formulate optimization problems with linear constraints?

plain_explanation.example: Decide how much to produce of each product with limited machine hours.

name: Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) / Gaussian AHP

Gaussian AHP is a variant that dispenses with the traditional consistency check via the consistency ratio (CR).

expected_input.question: How to rank alternatives according to multiple criteria?

plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When the decision involves subjective criteria and needs to be made transparent.

name: t-test (one-sample, two-sample, paired)
when_to_use: Compare the mean of one group against a reference value, or the means of two groups (independent or paired); metric dependent variable, approximately normal.
notes: Compares the mean of one group with a reference value, or the means of two groups, and tells whether the observed difference is large enough not to be mere chance. Applications: before/after a campaign; comparing the performance of two branches.

expected_input.question: Is the difference between the means of one or two groups statistically significant?

pdca_use: Check phase: compare an indicator before/after an action, or between two units, with an auditable numeric result (statistic and p-value), no free-form narrative.

plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When comparing two groups on a number (e.g., before and after).
plain_explanation.data_needed: A numeric column and one that splits the data into two groups (or two measurements of the same item).

name: ANOVA (one-way / factorial) and post-hoc (Tukey)
when_to_use: Compare the means of three or more groups at once; metric dependent variable, one or more categorical factors; post-hoc (Tukey) shows which pairs differ.

pdca_use: Check phase: compare the same indicator across three or more units/shifts/periods at once, with post-hoc showing which pairs differ — closed-form calculation, no model selection.

plain_explanation.purpose: Checks whether three or more groups have truly different means.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When comparing several versions, classes or regions on a number.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A numeric column and a group column with 3+ categories.
plain_explanation.example: Compare the average sales of 4 regions.
plain_explanation.diagram: A  B  C  D -> does any mean stand out? -> which ones?

name: Non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon, Kruskal-Wallis)
when_to_use: Same group comparisons as the t-test/ANOVA, when the dependent variable is not normally distributed or the sample is small; ordinal or non-normal metric data.
notes: The same group comparisons as the t-test/ANOVA, but without requiring the data to follow a normal distribution. Applications: data with outliers or small samples, common in internal surveys.

expected_input.question: Do the groups differ when normality cannot be assumed?

pdca_use: Check phase: same before/after or between-group comparison when the indicator is not normally distributed (common in small PDCA datasets) — still a deterministic calculation.

plain_explanation.purpose: Compare groups without assuming the data have a 'normal' shape.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When the sample is small, has extreme values or is a ranking (score from 1 to 5).
plain_explanation.data_needed: A column of values or ranks and a group column.
plain_explanation.example: Compare satisfaction scores between two stores.
plain_explanation.diagram: values -> become ranks (1st, 2nd...) -> compare ranks between groups

name: Chi-square (independence / goodness of fit)
when_to_use: Two categorical variables arranged in a contingency table; test whether they are associated (independence) or whether an observed distribution matches an expected one (goodness of fit).
notes: Checks whether two categorical variables (e.g., gender x product preference) are related or whether it is coincidence. Applications: satisfaction survey cross-tabulated with customer profile.

expected_input.question: Are two categorical variables associated, or is it coincidence?

pdca_use: Check phase: verify whether the distribution of a cause/category (e.g., type of nonconformity) changed after the action, or whether two categorical causes are associated.

plain_explanation.purpose: Checks whether two categorical variables are related or independent.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When two categories are cross-tabulated and you want to know whether the link is real.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A table of counts crossing two categorical columns.
plain_explanation.example: See whether the acquisition channel influences the type of plan chosen.
plain_explanation.diagram: observed vs. expected if there were no relationship -> large difference = relationship

name: Correlation (Pearson / Spearman) with significance test
when_to_use: Two metric variables (Pearson, linear relationship) or at least ordinal ones (Spearman, monotonic relationship); measure the strength and test the significance of the association before other modeling.
notes: Measures whether two numeric variables rise and fall together, and whether that relationship is strong enough to trust. Applications: check whether marketing spend tracks sales before running a regression.

expected_input.question: Do two numeric variables vary together, and is the relationship strong enough to trust?

pdca_use: Plan/Check phase: measure whether two indicators vary together (and how much) before proposing an action — auditable diagnosis, not a predictive model.

plain_explanation.purpose: Measures how much two things vary together, from -1 to +1.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When you want to know whether two numbers move together, without claiming that one causes the other.
plain_explanation.data_needed: Two or more numeric columns.
plain_explanation.example: See whether ad spend and sales rise together.
plain_explanation.diagram: +1: rise together | 0: no relationship | -1: one rises, the other falls

name: Factor Analysis
when_to_use: Many metric variables correlated with each other (e.g., questionnaire items); reduce to a few latent factors that explain the common pattern, with adequacy checks (KMO, Bartlett's test of sphericity) before extraction.

expected_input.question: Which latent dimensions explain the correlation among many observed variables?

plain_explanation.purpose: Discovers a few hidden factors that explain the answers to many questions.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When several questions measure the same concept, such as satisfaction, and you want to confirm it.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A table with many correlated numeric columns, such as questionnaire scores.
plain_explanation.example: Reduce 15 survey questions to 3 dimensions: price, service, product.
plain_explanation.diagram: hidden factor -> reflects -> questions 1, 2, 3

name: Discriminant Analysis
when_to_use: Known, labeled groups; categorical dependent variable, metric predictors; classify new cases from the characteristics that best separate the groups.
notes: Uses known characteristics of already classified groups to predict which group a new case belongs to. Applications: classify customers as "high risk"/"low risk" for credit.

expected_input.question: Which known group does a new case most likely belong to?

plain_explanation.purpose: Creates a rule that separates already known groups using numeric measures.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When you want to classify new cases into existing groups and see what most differentiates the groups.
plain_explanation.data_needed: Numeric columns and a column with the known group.
plain_explanation.example: Distinguish good and bad payers by income, age and debts.
plain_explanation.diagram: two groups of points -> line that best separates them

name: MANOVA
when_to_use: Compare three or more groups on several metric dependent variables simultaneously, instead of running one ANOVA per variable.
notes: Like ANOVA, but compares several numeric outcomes at once across groups, instead of one by one. Applications: compare 3 marketing campaigns on sales, clicks and retention simultaneously.

expected_input.question: Do the groups differ when several metrics are evaluated together?

plain_explanation.purpose: Compares groups on several numbers at the same time, instead of one at a time.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When there is more than one outcome measure and you want a single verdict.
plain_explanation.data_needed: Several numeric outcome columns and a group column.
plain_explanation.example: Compare three teaching methods on reading and math scores together.
plain_explanation.diagram: groups A, B, C x measures 1, 2 -> do they differ overall?

name: Multidimensional Scaling (MDS)
when_to_use: (Dis)similarity matrix between items; represent the items on a low-dimensional map preserving the perceived relative distances.
notes: Turns a table of "how similar two items are" into a visual map where similar items sit close together. Applications: positioning map of competing brands from consumer perception.

expected_input.question: How to visualize, in a few dimensions, how similar or different the items are?

plain_explanation.purpose: Draws items on a map where distance on paper reflects similarity distance.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When you have similarities or distances between items and want to visualize them.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A table of distances/similarities between items, or numeric columns to compute them.
plain_explanation.example: Brand map according to customer perception.
plain_explanation.diagram: distance table -> 2D map: similar items sit close

name: Conjoint Analysis
when_to_use: Product/service described by combinable attributes and levels; respondents rate combinations; decompose total preference into the contribution of each attribute.
notes: Decomposes customer preference for a product into the contributions of each characteristic (price, brand, color). Applications: decide which attribute combination maximizes purchase intent.

expected_input.question: How much does each attribute of a product contribute to customer preference?

plain_explanation.purpose: Discovers what people value most in a product, from choices among bundles.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When you need to know how much price, brand or lead time weigh in the purchase decision.
plain_explanation.data_needed: Answers from people ranking or choosing among attribute combinations.
plain_explanation.example: Find out whether the customer prefers to pay less or receive sooner.
plain_explanation.diagram: bundle A (cheap, slow) vs. bundle B (expensive, fast) -> weight of each attribute

name: SARIMA (seasonal ARIMA)
when_to_use: Time series with a clear seasonal component (monthly/quarterly cycle) in addition to trend and autocorrelation; extension of the already cataloged ARIMA (12-arima) with seasonal terms (P,D,Q)m.
notes: Extension of the already cataloged ARIMA for when the pattern repeats in cycles (month, quarter). Applications: sales with year-end seasonality; energy consumption by season.

expected_input.question: How to forecast a time series whose pattern repeats in cycles?

plain_explanation.purpose: Forecasts series with strong periodic repetition (monthly, weekly) in addition to trend.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When the series has clear seasonality and you want a classical statistical model.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A column of values over time, regular, with several complete cycles.
plain_explanation.example: Forecast energy consumption month by month.
plain_explanation.diagram: series = trend + repeating cycle + remainder

name: VAR Models / Granger Causality
when_to_use: Two or more time series that potentially influence each other; model them jointly and test whether past values of one help predict another.
notes: Models several time series that influence each other and tests whether one helps predict another. Applications: check whether media spend today explains sales in the following weeks.

expected_input.question: Does one time series help predict another, and in which direction?

plain_explanation.purpose: Analyzes several series together and tests whether the past of one helps predict another.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When you want to know whether one series drives another in time, without proving real causation.
plain_explanation.data_needed: Two or more series columns over the same period and frequency.
plain_explanation.example: See whether a change in ads precedes a change in sales.
plain_explanation.diagram: series A (past) ->? series B (future)

name: GARCH
when_to_use: Financial/risk time series whose volatility varies over time (conditional heteroskedasticity); model the variance, not only the mean level.
notes: Models how volatility varies over time, not only the mean value. Applications: financial risk, commodity prices, series with variable "turbulence".

expected_input.question: How does the volatility of a series vary over time?

plain_explanation.purpose: Models the variation (volatility) of a series, which tends to come in calm and agitated waves.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When the interest is risk, not the value itself.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A column of values or returns over time, many points.
plain_explanation.example: Estimate the daily volatility of a financial asset.
plain_explanation.diagram: calm ~~~ agitated ^^^ calm ~~~ (variation also has memory)

name: STL Decomposition
when_to_use: Time series to be diagnosed before choosing a model (ETS/ARIMA/Prophet); separate into trend, seasonality and residual in a way that is robust to outliers.
notes: Separates a time series into trend, seasonality and residual, visually and robustly to outliers. Applications: quick diagnosis before choosing among the already cataloged time-series models (12-suavizacao-exponencial-ets, 12-arima, 12-prophet).

expected_input.question: What are the trend, seasonality and residual of a time series?

pdca_use: Plan/Check phase: separate an indicator into trend, seasonality and residual before deciding whether a variation is a special cause or an expected seasonal pattern — closed-form decomposition, not a forecast.

plain_explanation.purpose: Separates a series into trend, seasonal cycle and remainder.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When you want to understand the series before forecasting, or remove seasonality.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A column of values over time, with regular period and at least 2 cycles.
plain_explanation.example: Separate the year-end rise from the real sales trend.
plain_explanation.diagram: series = trend + seasonality + residual

name: Regularization (Ridge / Lasso / Elastic Net)
when_to_use: Linear/logistic regression with many candidate predictors and risk of overfitting or multicollinearity; penalizes large coefficients (Ridge), zeroes out the least useful (Lasso) or combines both (Elastic Net).
notes: Versions of linear regression that penalize barely useful variables, avoiding a "memorized" model and helping to select predictors. Applications: many candidate variables and few observations (e.g., survey data).

expected_input.question: Which predictors really matter when there are many candidates and a risk of overfitting?

plain_explanation.purpose: Does regression with many factors 'taming' weights so as not to memorize noise.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When there are many factors, some redundant, and ordinary regression becomes unstable.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A table with a numeric response and many factor columns.
plain_explanation.example: Predict real-estate prices with 50 features, selecting the ones that matter.
plain_explanation.diagram: many factors -> penalize large weights -> few factors remain (Lasso zeroes)

name: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
when_to_use: Classification or regression by similarity; categorical or metric dependent variable, metric/scaled predictors, no assumption of functional form.
notes: Classifies or predicts a new case by looking at the most similar already-known cases. Applications: simple recommendation, diagnosis by profile similarity.

expected_input.question: What is the expected class or value of a new case, looking at the most similar already-known cases?

plain_explanation.purpose: Classifies or predicts by looking at the most similar already-known neighbors.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When 'those who are alike behave alike' makes sense and the dataset is small.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A table with numeric factors and the known response of each case.
plain_explanation.example: Predict a new customer's plan from the 5 most similar customers.
plain_explanation.diagram: new point -> 5 nearest neighbors -> majority decides

name: Support Vector Machine (SVM)
when_to_use: Binary classification (or multiclass via extension) with a not necessarily linear boundary between classes (kernel); seeks the maximum separation margin between groups.
notes: Finds the "dividing line" that separates two classes with the largest possible safety margin. Applications: binary classification with a non-obvious boundary between groups.

expected_input.question: What is the boundary that separates two classes with the largest possible safety margin?

plain_explanation.purpose: Finds the boundary that best separates two classes, with the most room possible.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When there are two classes and many factors, with a medium dataset.
plain_explanation.data_needed: Numeric factor columns and a response with two classes.
plain_explanation.example: Separate spam and non-spam emails.
plain_explanation.diagram: class A  ooo | line with margin | xxx  class B

name: Naive Bayes (general classification, beyond text)
when_to_use: Classification with categorical (or discretized) predictors, few observations, assuming conditional independence between predictors given the class; complements 22-classificacao-texto-naive-bayes beyond the document-term matrix.
notes: The catalog already has Naive Bayes for text; the general version applies the same probabilistic logic to any categorical variable. Applications: fast classification with few observations and categorical variables, outside the text domain.

expected_input.question: What is the most probable class of a case, combining the probability of each characteristic?

plain_explanation.purpose: Estimates the chance of each category by adding up the evidence from each factor, simply and quickly.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When you want a fast classifier, even with few examples.
plain_explanation.data_needed: Factor columns (numbers or categories) and the known category.
plain_explanation.example: Predict whether a ticket is urgent from its characteristics.
plain_explanation.diagram: evidence 1 x evidence 2 x ... -> chance per category

name: Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM)
when_to_use: Clustering when groups may overlap; instead of hard assignment (like k-means, already cataloged in 05-clustering-nao-hierarquico), estimates the probability of each case belonging to each group.
notes: Clustering that, instead of hard groups, gives the probability of each case belonging to each group. Applications: customer segmentation with overlapping profiles.

expected_input.question: What is the probability of a case belonging to each of several latent groups?

plain_explanation.purpose: Groups items allowing each to belong partially to several groups.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When groups overlap and you want a probability, not just a label.
plain_explanation.data_needed: Numeric table, one item per row.
plain_explanation.example: Segment customers who sit between two profiles.
plain_explanation.diagram: item: 70% group A, 30% group B

name: t-SNE / UMAP
when_to_use: Data with many dimensions (dozens to hundreds of variables); reduce to 2D/3D preserving local neighborhood for visualization, not for downstream modeling.
notes: Reduce many-dimensional data to 2D/3D to see patterns and clusters by eye. Applications: visualize customer or product clusters before running k-means/hierarchical.

expected_input.question: How to visualize in 2D/3D a pattern that only exists in many dimensions?

plain_explanation.purpose: Draws data with many columns on a plane, keeping neighbors together, to see groups.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When you want to visually explore a complex dataset.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A numeric table with many columns.
plain_explanation.example: See natural clusters of documents or customers on a chart.
plain_explanation.diagram: hundreds of dimensions -> [projection] -> 2D map

name: Association Rules (Apriori / Market Basket)
when_to_use: Transactions with item sets (e.g., shopping cart); find item combinations that appear together more often than a minimum support/confidence.
notes: Finds item combinations that tend to appear together in the same transaction. Applications: "customers who buy X also buy Y" in retail/e-commerce.

expected_input.question: Which items tend to appear together in the same transaction?

plain_explanation.purpose: Discovers what tends to appear together ('whoever takes A also takes B').
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When there are item lists per transaction and you want to find frequent combinations.
plain_explanation.data_needed: List of transactions, each with the items it contains.
plain_explanation.example: Discover which products are bought together.
plain_explanation.diagram: {bread, milk} -> butter (confidence 70%)

name: Survival Analysis (Kaplan-Meier, Cox)
when_to_use: The dependent variable is the time until an event (which may not have occurred for all cases — censoring); Kaplan-Meier estimates the survival curve, Cox models the effect of covariates on the event hazard.
notes: Models the time until an event happens (churn, failure, death) and measures the effect of factors on that time. Applications: time until subscription cancellation; time until equipment failure.

expected_input.question: How long until an event occurs, and which factors speed it up or delay it?

plain_explanation.purpose: Estimates how long it takes for an event to happen, even when some cases have not finished yet.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When the time until something happens matters: cancellation, failure, return.
plain_explanation.data_needed: For each item: observed time, whether the event occurred or not, and factors.
plain_explanation.example: Estimate how long a customer stays before canceling.

name: Anomaly Detection (Isolation Forest, LOF, One-Class SVM)
when_to_use: Identify rare/atypical cases with no (or few) labeled examples of anomalies; learns the "normal" pattern of the data and flags what deviates.
notes: Learns the "normal" pattern of the data and flags the cases that deviate too much from it. Applications: transaction fraud, sensor failure, audit outliers.

expected_input.question: Which cases deviate too much from the normal pattern of the data?

plain_explanation.purpose: Flags cases very different from the pattern that deserve attention.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When looking for fraud, errors or rare failures.
plain_explanation.data_needed: Numeric table, one case per row, in reasonable volume.
plain_explanation.example: Find out-of-pattern expenses in a spending dataset.
plain_explanation.diagram: cloud of normal points + a few isolated points = anomalies

name: Difference-in-Differences (DiD)
when_to_use: Intervention applied to one group at a point in time, with a comparable unaffected control group; compare the change (before→after) between the two groups to isolate the effect of the intervention.
notes: Compares the change in a group that received an intervention with the change in a similar group that did not, isolating the real effect. Applications: measure the impact of a policy/campaign by comparing before/after with a control group.

expected_input.question: What is the causal effect of an intervention, isolated from trends that already existed?

pdca_use: Check/Act phase: isolate the causal effect of an action implemented in a group/unit by comparing its change with an unaffected control unit — closed-form calculation (difference of means), but the parallel-trends assumption must be checked before use; cite this caveat to the user.

plain_explanation.purpose: Estimates the effect of a change by comparing who was affected with who was not, before and after.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When an intervention hit part of the cases and random assignment is not possible.
plain_explanation.data_needed: Outcome measure in two groups (affected and not), before and after.
plain_explanation.example: Measure the effect of a new policy in one region using another as reference.
plain_explanation.diagram: (after-before of affected group) - (after-before of reference group)

name: Propensity Score Matching
when_to_use: Evaluate the effect of a treatment/program without random assignment; match treated and untreated cases with a similar profile (probability of treatment) before comparing the outcome.
notes: Matches treated and untreated cases with a similar profile to compare outcomes as if it were an experiment. Applications: evaluate the effect of a program/training without a random control group.

expected_input.question: What would the outcome of the treated have been had they not been treated, using similar cases as the counterfactual?

plain_explanation.purpose: Compares treated and untreated cases that were similar from the start, to isolate the treatment effect.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When there was no random assignment and the groups differ in profile.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A 'treated/not' column, the outcome and profile factors for each case.
plain_explanation.example: Measure the effect of a course on salary by comparing similar people.
plain_explanation.diagram: each treated -> similar untreated match -> compare outcomes

name: Design of Experiments / A/B Testing
when_to_use: Decide between two or more versions of something (page, email, process) before scaling; random assignment to groups and statistical comparison of the result.
notes: Formalizes how to split groups and measure the outcome so that cause and effect can be claimed with statistical confidence. Applications: test two versions of a page, email or process before scaling.

expected_input.question: How to design and measure an experiment so that cause and effect can be claimed with confidence?

pdca_use: Plan/Check phase: size the sample and statistically compare two versions of an action before scaling — closed-form formulas (proportions/sample size), no model fitting.

plain_explanation.purpose: Compares two randomly assigned versions (A and B) to see which works better, and plans the size of the test.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When you can randomly choose who sees what.
plain_explanation.data_needed: For each participant, the version received and the outcome (e.g., converted or not).
plain_explanation.example: Test which of two emails gets more replies.
plain_explanation.diagram: audience -> random draw -> version A | version B -> compare rates

name: Monte Carlo Simulation
when_to_use: The result depends on several uncertain variables with plausible ranges/distributions; generate thousands of random scenarios to estimate the distribution of the result and its risk.
notes: Tests thousands of random scenarios within plausible ranges to estimate the risk and variation of a result. Applications: cash-flow projection, project-duration estimation.

expected_input.question: What is the risk and variation range of a result, given that several inputs are uncertain?

pdca_use: Plan phase: project the risk/variation range of a result (e.g., duration, cost of an action) from explicit distributions provided by the planner — deterministic given the seed and parameters, does not learn patterns from data.

plain_explanation.purpose: Repeats a scenario with random draws thousands of times to see the range of possible outcomes.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When several factors are uncertain and you want the chance of each outcome.
plain_explanation.data_needed: Likely values (minimum, most likely, maximum) for each uncertainty.
plain_explanation.example: Estimate the chance of a project overrunning its deadline.
plain_explanation.diagram: draw values -> compute -> repeat 10,000x -> distribution of results

name: Integer Programming / Transportation and Assignment Problem
when_to_use: Optimization problem (complements 23-programacao-linear/23-metodo-simplex) where the solution must be in whole numbers (not fractional), or a classic distribution problem between origins and destinations at minimum cost.
notes: Complements the already cataloged Linear Programming/Simplex for when the solution must be in whole numbers (not fractional) or is a classic distribution problem. Applications: team allocation, routing, distribution between factories and distribution centers.

expected_input.question: What is the minimum-cost allocation/distribution, given that the solution must be integer?

pdca_use: Plan phase: minimum-cost allocation/distribution between origins and destinations (e.g., teams, inventory) when the solution must be in whole units — same deterministic nature as the Simplex.

plain_explanation.purpose: Plans what to ship from where to where at the lowest cost, in whole quantities.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When there are origins, destinations, route costs and limits.
plain_explanation.data_needed: Cost per route, supply of each origin and demand of each destination.
plain_explanation.example: Decide which factory supplies which distribution center.
plain_explanation.diagram: factories -> routes with cost -> centers (lowest total cost)

name: Control Charts (SPC) and Process Capability (Cp/Cpk)
when_to_use: Process measured repeatedly over time; control charts assess whether the process is stable (common vs. special causes), Cp/Cpk measure whether it is within acceptable specification limits.
notes: Tracks a process over time to see whether it is stable, and measures whether it is within acceptable limits. Applications: industrial quality control, operational indicator monitoring.

expected_input.question: Is the process stable over time, and within acceptable limits?

pdca_use: Direct fit for Check: control charts and Cp/Cpk are the classic SPC instrument for telling whether a process is stable and within specification — same logic as industrial PDCA, 100% deterministic calculation.

plain_explanation.purpose: Tracks a process over time and warns when it leaves its normal behavior.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When you want to monitor ongoing quality or performance.
plain_explanation.data_needed: Successive measurements of the process, in time order.
plain_explanation.example: Watch the daily response time and act when it leaves the band.
plain_explanation.diagram:
upper limit ---------
mean       ~~~~~~~~~
lower limit ---------

name: Spatial Analysis / Geostatistics
when_to_use: Data with geographic location (coordinates, municipality, region); account for the fact that nearby observations tend to be more alike (spatial autocorrelation) instead of treating each point as independent.

expected_input.question: How does the geographic location of each observation relate to the measured value?

plain_explanation.purpose: Analyzes data that has a place on the map, checking whether neighbors resemble each other.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When location matters for the outcome.
plain_explanation.data_needed: Values per location, with coordinates or a region identifier.
plain_explanation.example: See whether neighborhoods with a high incidence of a problem cluster together.
plain_explanation.diagram: map -> similar neighboring regions? -> clusters

name: Social Network Analysis / Graphs
when_to_use: Data representable as connections between entities (people, companies, items); measure centrality, distance and communities in the network formed by these connections.
notes: Maps connections between people/items and measures who is most central or which groups form in the network. Applications: customer referral network, informal org chart, co-authorship.

expected_input.question: Who is most central in the network, and which groups form in it?

plain_explanation.purpose: Studies connections between entities, finding the most central ones and the groups.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When the question is about who is connected to whom.
plain_explanation.data_needed: List of connected pairs (who links to whom), with optional weight.
plain_explanation.example: Find central suppliers in a purchasing network.
plain_explanation.diagram:
A--B--C
   |
   D (B is central)

name: Topic Modeling (LDA)
when_to_use: Large set of texts with no prior topic label; complements 21-text-mining-basico/22-tfidf by automatically inferring the latent topics that explain the vocabulary of the documents.
notes: Automatically finds the hidden "topics" in a large set of texts, with no prior label. Applications: discover recurring themes in open-ended survey answers.

expected_input.question: Which latent topics explain a large set of texts, with no prior label?

plain_explanation.purpose: Automatically discovers the subjects that appear in a set of texts.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When there are many texts and nobody can read them all.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A text column, one document per row, in large volume.
plain_explanation.example: Discover the themes of thousands of complaints.
plain_explanation.diagram: texts -> [LDA] -> topic 1 (words), topic 2 (words)...

name: Word Embeddings (Word2Vec / GloVe)
when_to_use: Need for semantic similarity between words/texts beyond term counts (complements 22-tfidf); represents words as numeric vectors where words with similar meaning end up close together.
notes: Represents words as numbers so that words with similar meaning are mathematically "close". Applications: semantic search, grouping similar answers even when different words are used.

expected_input.question: Which words/texts have similar meaning, even when using different words?

plain_explanation.purpose: Turns words into numbers so that similar meanings end up close together.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When you want the computer to understand that different words can mean the same thing.
plain_explanation.data_needed: A large set of texts to learn the relationships.
plain_explanation.example: Search documents by meaning, not only by the exact word.
plain_explanation.diagram: 'car' and 'automobile' end up close; 'banana' far away

name: Recommender Systems (collaborative filtering)
when_to_use: User-item interaction history (purchase, rating, click); suggest items to a user based on what similar users preferred.
notes: Suggests items to a user based on what similar users liked. Applications: product/content recommendation.

expected_input.question: What to recommend to a user, based on what similar users preferred?

plain_explanation.purpose: Suggests items to a person based on what similar people chose.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When there is a history of who consumed what and you want to suggest the next item.
plain_explanation.data_needed: Table with the person's identifier, the item's and, if available, the rating given.
plain_explanation.example: Suggest products to a customer based on what similar customers bought.
plain_explanation.diagram: you ~ similar people -> what they liked and you have not seen yet

name: Bayesian Statistics / Regression
when_to_use: Same question as a traditional regression, but with prior knowledge to incorporate and/or little data; the answer comes out as a probability distribution (explicit uncertainty), not just a point estimate.
notes: Same question as traditional regression, but incorporates prior knowledge and gives the uncertainty of the answer as a probability, not just a number. Applications: forecasting with little data, updating an estimate as new data arrive.

expected_input.question: What is the estimate and its uncertainty, incorporating prior knowledge?

plain_explanation.purpose: Updates an initial belief with the data, returning the chance of each possible value.
plain_explanation.when_to_use_plain: When there is useful prior knowledge or little data.
plain_explanation.data_needed: The observed data and a prior belief about what is expected.
plain_explanation.example: Estimate the conversion rate of a new campaign, starting from that of past campaigns.
plain_explanation.diagram: initial belief + new data = updated belief
